executiveSummary: Chapter 8 establishes the cost-basis approach to inventory valuation, covering how companies classify inventories, determine which goods and costs belong in inventory, and choose among allowable cost flow assumptions (specific identification, FIFO, and average-cost under IFRS). The chapter concludes that correct inventory measurement is critical because errors directly distort cost of goods sold, net income, working capital, and the current ratio across multiple periods.
keyTopics: Inventory classifications: Merchandising companies carry a single Inventory account, while manufacturers maintain three accounts — Raw Materials, Work in Process (WIP), and Finished Goods — each representing a different stage of the production cycle.

Inventory systems: A perpetual system continuously records every purchase and sale in the Inventory account and supports a Cost of Goods Sold account updated in real time; a periodic system defers cost determination to period-end through a physical count, computing COGS as a residual.

Goods included in inventory: Ownership (control/legal title) governs inclusion — goods in transit under f.o.b. shipping point belong to the buyer, consigned goods remain with the consignor, and product financing ('parking') arrangements keep inventory on the financing party's books.

Costs included in inventory: Product costs (purchase price, import duties, freight-in, conversion costs) are capitalised to inventory; period costs (selling, G&A, most interest) are expensed as incurred.

Cost flow assumptions: IFRS requires specific identification for non-interchangeable items and permits FIFO or average-cost (weighted-average for periodic; moving-average for perpetual) for all others. LIFO is prohibited under IFRS but discussed in Appendix 8A for completeness.

Comparative effects of cost flow methods: In a rising-price environment, FIFO produces the highest ending inventory and net income (but lowest cash retained after taxes), while average-cost falls in between; LIFO (Appendix) produces the lowest net income but highest cash retention.

Inventory errors: Understating ending inventory overstates COGS and understates net income in the current period; the error self-corrects (counterbalances) in the following period. Simultaneously omitting a purchase and its related ending inventory leaves COGS and net income unaffected but understates accounts payable and inventory, distorting the current ratio.

Treatment of purchase discounts: IFRS requires discounts to reduce inventory cost; under the gross method a separate Purchase Discounts account is used, while the preferred net method records inventory net of available discounts and isolates 'Purchase Discounts Lost' as a financial expense.

importantDefinitions.Inventories: Asset items held for sale in the ordinary course of business, or goods to be used or consumed in producing goods for sale.
importantDefinitions.Raw Materials Inventory: Costs assigned to materials on hand that have not yet been placed into the production process.
importantDefinitions.Work in Process (WIP) Inventory: The accumulated cost of raw materials, direct labour, and allocated manufacturing overhead for units that have been started but not yet completed.
importantDefinitions.Finished Goods Inventory: Costs identified with completed but unsold units on hand at the end of the fiscal period.
importantDefinitions.Perpetual Inventory System: A system that continuously records every purchase and sale in the Inventory account, maintaining an up-to-date balance and a running Cost of Goods Sold figure.
importantDefinitions.Periodic Inventory System: A system that records purchases in a Purchases account and determines both ending inventory and COGS only at period-end through a physical count.
importantDefinitions.Product Costs: Costs that attach to inventory — including purchase price, import duties, freight-in, and conversion costs — and are capitalised in the Inventory account until the goods are sold.
importantDefinitions.Period Costs: Costs indirectly related to the acquisition or production of goods (e.g., selling expense, G&A) that are expensed in the period incurred rather than capitalised to inventory.
importantDefinitions.FIFO (First-In, First-Out): A cost flow assumption that the first goods purchased are the first sold, so ending inventory reflects the most recent purchase prices.
importantDefinitions.Weighted-Average Cost Method: A periodic inventory cost flow method that divides the total cost of goods available for sale by total units available to derive a single average unit cost applied to all sales and ending inventory.

accountingTreatments: Perpetual system purchase entry: Dr Inventory / Cr Accounts Payable (freight-in also debited to Inventory, not a separate account).
Perpetual system sale entry (two parts): Dr Accounts Receivable / Cr Sales Revenue AND Dr Cost of Goods Sold / Cr Inventory.
Perpetual inventory shrinkage adjustment when physical count is below book: Dr Inventory Over and Short / Cr Inventory (the debit flows to Cost of Goods Sold or Other expense).

Periodic system — end-of-period COGS computation: Beginning Inventory + Purchases + Freight-In - Purchase Returns & Allowances - Purchase Discounts = Cost of Goods Available for Sale; subtract physical Ending Inventory to derive COGS.

Purchase discounts — gross method: Purchase recorded at gross invoice; discount taken is credited to Purchase Discounts (contra-purchases). Net method: Purchase recorded net; failure to take discount is Dr Purchase Discounts Lost / Cr Cash (reported as financial expense).

Sales with repurchase (parking) arrangements: Inventory and related liability remain on the seller's books because control has not transferred; no revenue is recognised until the repurchase agreement is resolved.
criticalFormulas: Cost of Goods Sold (periodic) = Beginning Inventory + Cost of Goods Purchased - Ending Inventory. Example: €600 + €5,400 - €2,400 = €3,600 COGS.
Weighted-Average Unit Cost = Total Cost of Goods Available for Sale / Total Units Available. Example (Call-Mart): €43,900 / 10,000 units = €4.39 per unit; Ending Inventory = 6,000 × €4.39 = €26,340.
Moving-Average Unit Cost (perpetual) = Running Total Cost / Running Total Units after each purchase. Example: after March 15 purchase, €34,400 / 8,000 units = €4.30 per unit for the next withdrawal.
FIFO Ending Inventory = Units on hand priced from most recent purchase layers backward. Example (Call-Mart periodic): 2,000 @ €4.75 + 4,000 @ €4.40 = €9,500 + €17,600 = €27,100.
Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities. Illustration 8.17: with understated payables/inventory ($40,000 omitted) ratio = $120,000 / $40,000 = 3:1 vs. correct $160,000 / $80,000 = 2:1.
illustrativeExample: Call-Mart SpA (March): purchases 2,000 units @ €4.00, 6,000 @ €4.40, 2,000 @ €4.75; sells 4,000 units; ending inventory = 6,000 units. Under FIFO (periodic): ending inventory = 2,000 @ €4.75 + 4,000 @ €4.40 = €27,100; COGS = €43,900 - €27,100 = €16,800. Under weighted-average (periodic): avg cost = €43,900 / 10,000 = €4.39; ending inventory = 6,000 × €4.39 = €26,340; COGS = €43,900 - €26,340 = €17,560. Under moving-average (perpetual): after March 15 purchase, avg = €4.30; March 19 withdrawal cost = 4,000 × €4.30 = €17,200; after March 30 purchase, new avg = €4.45; ending inventory = 6,000 × €4.45 = €26,700.
disclosurePresentationNotes: Inventory classification: Companies must disclose the composition of inventory (raw materials, WIP, finished goods for manufacturers; single merchandise inventory for retailers) on the face of the statement of financial position or in the notes.

Cost flow method: The cost flow assumption (FIFO or average-cost) must be disclosed and applied consistently; any change in method requires explanation and disclosure of its financial statement effect.

Consigned goods and special arrangements: Material amounts of consigned goods held by or sent to third parties, and the nature of any product financing (repurchase) arrangements, should be disclosed in the notes.

Inventory errors and restatements: When an inventory error is discovered that affects prior periods, the financial statements for those periods must be restated and the nature and amount of the error disclosed.
potentialPitfalls: Confusing legal title with control for transit goods: Goods shipped f.o.b. destination are still owned by the seller while in transit and must NOT be included in the buyer's year-end inventory count; failing to check shipping terms leads to under- or overstatement of both inventory and purchases.

Assuming inventory errors are immaterial or self-correcting in year one: Although an ending inventory understatement counterbalances in the next period, both years' income statements are individually misstated; management cannot dismiss the error simply because the two-year total net income is correct.

Conflating FIFO's balance sheet strength with income statement accuracy: FIFO reports ending inventory close to current replacement cost, but it charges older (lower) costs against current revenue in a rising-price environment, overstating gross profit and creating a 'phantom profit' that may lead to inadequate pricing or dividend decisions.
